credit.credit-words: Modulation
a bit of theory
BH
Modulation means changing key. In Common Practice (classical theory up to the mid-19th Century) the idea
was to try to make this change as smooth as possible, to avoid jarring the listener's ear. In modern times we
have come to accept more abrupt modulations, but the older techniques are still useful, particularly in writing
melodies. I'll try to cover all of the types of modulation here.
1. Pivot Chords
To modulate smoothly between closely related keys (keys that differ by at most two sharps or flats) it is normal
to identify chords that are common to both keys and to use them as pivot chords between the two keys.
Here are some examples. Of course you can transpose these into other pairs of keys.
2. Pivot Chords Between Remote Keys
Beyond two sharps or flats difference, there are no common chords. To modulate using pivot chords between
more remote keys, there are two possibile approaches, and you can use a combination of both.
2a. modulate via intermediate keys
Find a key "between" the two keys, modulate to that first, then modulate again to the target.
2b. admit more exotic chords
Apart from the standard chords of a key, there are a number of additional "honorary members" that can be used
as pivot chords just as easily. There are too many to enumerate here, but a few are particularly noteworthy.
3. Pivot Tones
Even though remote keys don't have simple common chords, they will always have at least a few common notes,
and they can serve to ease the transition. Again there are innumerable examples for you to find on your own, I'm
only going to show one.
4. Modulation by Sequence
Having established a harmonic/melodic fragment, repeat it in the new key.
